experiments.title: Cantor's diagonal trick on a finite list
experiments.summary: Builds the diagonal-flipped sequence for a fixed list of 8 infinite binary sequences and checks exactly that it differs from every listed sequence. The finite run illustrates the mechanism only; the proof that the infinite binary sequences cannot be listed is Cantor's general argument.

experiments.title: Clock arithmetic: which residues have inverses?
experiments.summary: Prints the addition and multiplication tables mod 6, finds by search which residues have multiplicative inverses mod 6 and mod 7, and checks for every k from 2 to 30 that these are exactly the a with gcd(a, k) = 1. The table proves the pattern only for k <= 30; for every k it is a theorem (from Bezout's identity) proved elsewhere.

experiments.title: Sorting and counting a market basket
experiments.summary: Sorts a fixed basket of market items by kind and by colour and counts each group exactly, then checks every one of the 720 orders of a 6-item basket gives the same counts. This proves order-independence for that basket only; why it holds for every finite collection is explained in the lesson, not by this program.

experiments.title: Composing functions: associative, but order matters
experiments.summary: Checks associativity of composition on all 19683 triples of functions on a 3-element set and the identity laws on all 27 functions (a proof for that set only), and finds functions with g o f != f o g, a counterexample showing composition is not commutative in general.

experiments.title: Counting functions, injections and surjections
experiments.summary: Lists every function between sets of sizes 1 to 4, counts the injective, surjective and bijective ones exactly, and compares the counts with n^m, the falling factorial and the inclusion-exclusion formula. Agreement for these sizes is proved by enumeration; that the formulas hold for all sizes is a theorem the enumeration does not establish.

experiments.title: Forty primes in a row, then a counterexample
experiments.summary: Tests n^2 + n + 41 for primality (exact trial division) for n = 0 to 39, where every value is prime, then finds the first failure at n = 40, where the value is 41 * 41. Forty confirming cases were evidence, not proof; one counterexample settles the question.

experiments.title: Exact versus numerical: 0.1 + 0.2 and the square root of 2
experiments.summary: Compares 0.1 + 0.2 in floating point with exact fractions, shows how rounding error accumulates when 0.1 is added 10000 times in float64 and float32, and computes the square root of 2 by Newton's method (approximate) and with sympy.sqrt(2) (exact). Numerical results are approximations whose error must be measured; exact and symbolic results involve no rounding.

experiments.title: Hunting for inverses in the integers and the rationals
experiments.summary: Searches a finite window of integers for additive and multiplicative inverses (every additive inverse is found; multiplicative ones only for 1 and -1), then checks exactly with fractions that every non-zero rational has an inverse. A finite search is experimental evidence; the short size argument printed at the end is what proves that no other integer has a multiplicative inverse.

experiments.title: Does a random walk come home? Statistical evidence
experiments.summary: Simulates 4000 seeded random walks on the integers, estimates the chance of returning to 0 within 2, 10, 100 and 1000 steps with 95% confidence intervals, and compares with the exact formula 1 - C(2m, m)/4^m. Agreement is statistical evidence, which can never be certain and cannot show that a return eventually happens with probability 1 (Polya's theorem).

experiments.title: Remainder families: residue classes that add up
experiments.summary: Splits the integers -12..12 into residue classes mod k, checks for k = 1 to 12 that the classes are disjoint and cover the range, and that the class of a sum or product depends only on the classes of the inputs, for every choice of representatives in that range. This is evidence for the general theorem, not a proof of it; a counterexample shows powers do not respect classes in the exponent.

experiments.title: Checking set identities exhaustively
experiments.summary: Checks De Morgan's laws and both distributive laws on every pair or triple of subsets of a 4-element universe (a proof for that universe only, not for all sets), and finds the smallest counterexample to A - (B - C) = (A - B) - C, which does disprove that 'law' for sets in general.

experiments.title: Negative times negative: grid, symbols and proof
experiments.summary: Checks (-a)(-b) = ab and (-a)b = -(ab) on a 21 x 21 grid of integers (evidence for those cases only), then lets SymPy confirm the identities symbolically, which relies on the ring rules SymPy has built in. Neither explains why the rule holds: the lesson's proof from the distributive law does.
